root.title: Software Architecture
root.text: Software architecture is the set of high-level structural decisions in a codebase — how it's divided into modules, what depends on what, where boundaries sit — that are expensive to change later. Good architecture doesn't prevent all bugs, but it determines how easily a codebase can grow without collapsing under its own complexity.

children.title: Design Patterns
children.text: Design patterns (Factory, Observer, Strategy, and others) are named, reusable solutions to recurring design problems, giving engineers a shared vocabulary to discuss structure without re-deriving it each time. They're tools, not mandates — misapplying a pattern where a simpler solution would do is a common source of unnecessary complexity.

children.title: Domain-Driven Design
children.text: Domain-Driven Design structures code around the business domain itself — using the same language the business uses, and drawing module boundaries ('bounded contexts') around real business concepts rather than technical layers. It's especially valuable in complex business domains where the biggest risk is engineers and stakeholders silently meaning different things by the same word.

children.title: Clean Architecture & Layering
children.text: Layered architectures separate business logic from infrastructure concerns (databases, frameworks, UI) so the core logic can be tested and changed without dragging along everything it happens to be plugged into. The dependency direction — infrastructure depends on business logic, never the reverse — is the detail most implementations get wrong.
